pages.text: On a playground see-saw, a small child can balance a much bigger one. The trick is where they sit. The small child sits far from the middle, and the big child sits close to it. A see-saw is a lever: a stiff bar that turns about a fixed point called the pivot, or fulcrum. The turning effect of a force is called its moment. Moment = force × distance from the pivot. A small force far from the pivot can have the same moment as a large force close to it. That is why the see-saw balances.

pages.text: Every lever has a pivot, a load to be moved, and an effort, which is the force you apply. Levers are grouped into three classes by which of these is in the middle. In a first-class lever, the pivot is in the middle, as in a see-saw, a crowbar, or a pair of scissors. In a second-class lever, the load is in the middle, as in a wheelbarrow or a bottle opener. In a third-class lever, the effort is in the middle, as in a pair of tongs, a fishing rod, or a broom. Your own forearm is a third-class lever, with the elbow as its pivot.

pages.text: Most levers help us lift a heavy load with a small effort. But a lever can also be used the other way round: a large force moving a short distance can make the far end move a long distance, very fast. Hundreds of years ago, before cannons, armies used this idea to throw heavy stones at castle walls. The machine was called a trebuchet (say TREB-yoo-shay). It had a long wooden beam on a pivot. A very heavy box of rocks, the counterweight, hung from the short end. A sling holding a stone was tied to the long end.

pages.alt: A labelled diagram of a wooden trebuchet showing the beam, pivot, counterweight on the short arm, and sling on the long arm.

pages.text: Soldiers pulled the long end down, which raised the counterweight high into the air. When they let go, the counterweight dropped and the beam swung round. Both ends of the beam turn through the same angle in the same time. But the long end travels round a much bigger circle, so it moves much faster. If the long arm is four times the length of the short arm, its tip moves four times as fast. The sling made the arm longer still. At the top of the swing the sling opened, and the stone flew off towards its target.

pages.text: A trebuchet is also a lesson in energy. An object lifted high above the ground stores gravitational potential energy. The heavier the object and the higher it is lifted, the more energy it stores. When the counterweight falls, this stored energy changes into kinetic energy, the energy of movement, in the beam and the stone. As the stone rises through the air it slows, and some kinetic energy becomes potential energy again. As it falls, it speeds up. When it hits the wall, its energy does work breaking the stone and is spread out as heat and sound. Energy is never destroyed. It only changes form.

pages.text: The largest trebuchets could throw a stone as heavy as two grown men over a distance of two or three football pitches. Would a heavier stone or a faster stone do more damage? Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed, but speed counts for more. Doubling the mass doubles the energy. Doubling the speed makes the energy four times as great. Today trebuchets are built only for sport and for physics lessons, but the rule still matters every day. A car at 100 km/h carries four times the kinetic energy of the same car at 50 km/h. That is why speeding makes crashes so deadly.

activities.question: What is the moment of a force?
options: The turning effect of the force: force × distance from the pivot
The time for which the force acts

activities.question: A wheelbarrow is a second-class lever. What lies between the pivot and the effort?
What energy change takes place as the counterweight falls?
options: Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy
Heat energy changes into potential energy
Kinetic energy changes into chemical energy

activities.question: Apply it: A 20 kg child sits 3 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Where must a 30 kg child sit on the other side to balance it?

activities.prompt: Arrange the energy changes in the order they happen.
items: Soldiers pull the long arm down, raising the counterweight.
The raised counterweight stores gravitational potential energy.
The counterweight falls, changing potential into kinetic energy.
The stone flies through the air with kinetic energy.
The stone hits the wall, turning energy into heat and sound.

glossary.definition: A stiff bar that turns about a fixed point.
The fixed point about which a lever turns; also called the fulcrum.
The turning effect of a force: force × distance from the pivot.
The force applied to a lever.
Gravitational potential energy: energy stored in an object because it has been raised above the ground.
Kinetic energy: the energy an object has because it is moving.
